quote_en: Now He did not teach us these things as being opposed to the law, but as fulfilling the law, and implanting in us the varied righteousness of the law. That would have been contrary to the law, if He had commanded His disciples to do anything which the law had prohibited. But this which He did command — namely, not only to abstain from things forbidden by the law, but even from longing after them — is not contrary to [the law], as I have remarked, neither is it the utterance of one destroying the law, but of one fulfilling, extending, and affording greater scope to it.
from_: Now He did not teach us
to: and affording greater scope to it.
keys: as being opposed to the law, but as fulfilling the law
fulfilling, extending, and affording greater scope to it
context: Irenaeus is arguing against Marcion that the one God is author of both Testaments. Here, on the Sermon on the Mount antitheses (Mt 5:21-44), he says Christ's 'you have heard... but I say' does not overturn the Law but extends it. Paragraphs 2-3 then describe the Law as laid down for those in bondage, which the Word later freed the soul from.
caveat: Translation: Roberts & Rambaut (ANF 1, 1885) as on New Advent (edited by K. Knight). Bracketed words [the law] are the translators'. This is about Christ's moral teaching, not about the penalties of the Law; it is the core of the D theme.

quote_en: The laws of bondage, however, were one by one promulgated to the people by Moses, suited for their instruction or for their punishment, as Moses himself declared: And the Lord commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and judgments. Deuteronomy 4:14 These things, therefore, which were given for bondage, and for a sign to them, He cancelled by the new covenant of liberty.
from_: The laws of bondage, however, were
to: by the new covenant of liberty.
keys: These things, therefore, which were given for bondage
He cancelled by the new covenant of liberty
context: Irenaeus argues that circumcision, Sabbaths and the other Mosaic ceremonies were 'a sign' and not the completion of righteousness, and that the Decalogue (the natural law) was never cancelled. Section 5 then says the Mosaic 'laws of bondage' were given to a people in servitude and were cancelled by the new covenant of liberty.
caveat: Adverse clause in the same paragraph: the laws were 'suited for their instruction or for their punishment' (the Deuteronomy 4:14 citation is for the statutes and judgments given through Moses). The same passage says the natural precepts and the Decalogue were 'increased and widened' rather than abolished. Chapter headings are editorial. Irenaeus does NOT say Christians must carry out any penalty.

quote_en: God made man a free [agent] from the beginning, possessing his own power, even as he does his own soul, to obey the behests (ad utendum sententia) of God voluntarily, and not by compulsion of God. For there is no coercion with God, but a good will [towards us] is present with Him continually.
to: us] is present with Him continually.
keys: there is no coercion with God
context: Chapter 37 argues that man has free will and that God does not force obedience. It opens by quoting the Lord's words 'How often would I have gathered thy children together, and thou wouldest not', and then says God made man free to obey voluntarily. Later in the same paragraph he says the disobedient 'shall receive condign punishment' from God.
caveat: Irenaeus does NOT say here that heretics must not be killed or coerced by the Church or the State; the statement is about God's relation to man. It is an argument by analogy for the persuasion model, not an explicit rule on human coercion, so it is not as direct as the brief hopes. The same chapter states that disobedient persons 'shall receive condign punishment' from God (see X caveat).

ref: Eusebius, Church History V.24.14-15 (Irenaeus's letter to Victor, quoted); Eusebius narration V.24.11
quote_en: Among these were the presbyters before Soter, who presided over the church which thou now rulest. We mean Anicetus, and Pius, and Hyginus, and Telesphorus, and Xystus. They neither observed it themselves, nor did they permit those after them to do so. And yet though not observing it, they were none the less at peace with those who came to them from the parishes in which it was observed; although this observance was more opposed to those who did not observe it. 15. But none were ever cast out on account of this form; but the presbyters before thee who did not observe it, sent the eucharist to those of other parishes who observed it.
from_: Among these were the presbyters before
to: of other parishes who observed it.
keys: But none were ever cast out on account of this form
sent the eucharist to those of other parishes who observed it
context: Eusebius (HE V.24.9) reports that Victor of Rome, over the date of Easter, tried to cut off the churches of Asia and declared the brethren excommunicate; Irenaeus, writing for the Gallic churches, rebuked Victor and urged that whole churches not be cut off over customs. The quoted letter is Irenaeus's own words, cited by Eusebius; Eusebius's narration (V.24.11, 'He fittingly admonishes Victor that he should not cut off whole churches') is Eusebius's paraphrase, not Irenaeus's.
caveat: Footnote markers [1710]-[1714] of the CCEL text removed; otherwise verbatim (NPNF2 translation, McGiffert, 1890). Greek not read. Dispute is ecclesial (excommunication over a calendar custom), not capital; it shows Irenaeus opposing excommunication of churches, not a general theory of religious liberty. Eusebius's own words are NOT in this quote.

quote_en: the priests in the temple profaned the Sabbath, and were blameless. Wherefore, then, were they blameless? Because when in the temple they were not engaged in secular affairs, but in the service of the Lord, fulfilling the law, but not going beyond it, as that man did, who of his own accord carried dry wood into the camp of God, and was justly stoned to death.
from_: the priests in the temple profaned
to: and was justly stoned to death.
keys: fulfilling the law, but not going beyond it
context: In ch. 8 Irenaeus defends the consistency of the Law and the Gospel, against Marcion, who said the Creator God was a different God. He argues that the priests in the Temple could break the Sabbath without guilt because they served the Lord's work, and contrasts a man who, acting on his own, carried wood into the camp and was stoned (Num 15:32-36).
caveat: ADVERSE: he calls a Mosaic capital sentence 'just' (for a Sabbath violation, of his own accord). He does NOT apply it to heretics or to Christians, and in the same passage he uses it to show the priests were blameless when acting within the Law. Death penalty under the OT law is approved as divine justice, not as a Christian norm.

quote_en: And the heretics, indeed, who bring strange fire to the altar of God — namely, strange doctrines— shall be burned up by the fire from heaven, as were Nadab and Abiud. Leviticus 10:1-2 But such as rise up in opposition to the truth, and exhort others against the Church of God, [shall] remain among those in hell (apud inferos), being swallowed up by an earthquake, even as those who were with Chore, Dathan, and Abiron. Numbers 16:33 But those who cleave asunder, and separate the unity of the Church, [shall] receive from God the same punishment as Jeroboam did.
from_: And the heretics, indeed, who bring
to: the same punishment as Jeroboam did.
keys: shall be burned up by the fire from heaven
receive from God the same punishment as Jeroboam did
context: In paragraph 2 of ch. 26 Irenaeus lists the groups that depart from the primitive succession and the Church's faith (heretics, schismatics, hypocrites, those who rise against the truth) and says what God will do to each. Paragraph 3 then turns to presbyters who serve their own lusts.
caveat: ADVERSE, but DIVINE: the burning of the heretics is a judgment that God will carry out ('burned up by the fire from heaven'), on the model of Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1-2, cited by Irenaeus as 'Nadab and Abiud'). Irenaeus does not say a human authority should burn or kill heretics, and the passage concerns future divine judgment. It is still a death-language statement about heretics and should be reported beside 4.8.3.

quote_en: Inasmuch, then, as in both Testaments there is the same righteousness of God [displayed] when God takes vengeance, in the one case indeed typically, temporarily, and more moderately; but in the other, really, enduringly, and more rigidly: for the fire is eternal, and the wrath of God which shall be revealed from heaven from the face of our Lord (as David also says, But the face of the Lord is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth ), entails a heavier punishment on those who incur it — the elders pointed out that those men are devoid of sense, who, [arguing] from what happened to those who formerly did not obey God, do endeavour to bring in another Father, setting over against [these punishments] what great things the Lord had done at His coming to save those who received Him, taking compassion upon them; while they keep silence with regard to His judgment; and all those things which shall come upon such as have heard His words, but done them not, and that it were better for them if they had not been born, Matthew 26:24
from_: Inasmuch, then, as in both Testaments
keys: in the one case indeed typically, temporarily, and more moderately
entails a heavier punishment on those who incur it
context: Ch. 28 answers those who exaggerate Christ's mercy and say a different God is revealed in the NT. Irenaeus says God's vengeance is the same in both Testaments, but in the Old it is 'typical' and temporary, in the New 'real' and eternal. He cites Mt 26:24 and Mt 10:15 on the judgment of those who have heard Christ's word and do not obey.
caveat: Compares OT and NT penalties a fortiori, as Heb 10:28-29 does, and the penalty is God's judgment, not the Church's. Irenaeus does NOT cite Heb 10:28 here; the comparison is his own. He also says 'the elders pointed out' the argument (an appeal to unnamed presbyters). It applies to those who 'have heard His words, but done them not', i.e. to Christians who disobey, not to a rule for coercing others.

quote_en: As then the unrighteous, the idolaters, and fornicators perished, so also is it now: for both the Lord declares, that such persons are sent into eternal fire; Matthew 25:41 and the apostle says, Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God? Be not deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, not effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 And as it was not to those who are without that he said these things, but to us, lest we should be cast forth from the kingdom of God, by doing any such thing, he proceeds to say, And such indeed were you; but you are washed, but you are sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and by the Spirit of our God.
from_: As then the unrighteous, the idolaters,
to: by the Spirit of our God.
keys: As then the unrighteous, the idolaters, and fornicators perished
lest we should be cast forth from the kingdom of God
context: Ch. 27 argues that the sins of the OT people were written down as a warning for Christians, and that the same God is judge in both Testaments. Irenaeus says the OT idolaters perished, and that the eternal fire awaits the unrighteous now, and he applies this to the Church members in 1 Cor 6:9-11.
caveat: The chapter heading (editorial) says 'lest the one and the same God... should bring down heavier upon us'; that wording is the translator's summary, not body text. Here he applies the OT punishment-warning to Christians (H), but still speaks of God's judgment. He also says those who lived viciously were 'cast out' and that the 'offending eye is plucked out' (church discipline, not capital).
